entries.title: Ex-Bears kicker Robbie Gould steps down as coach at St. Viator
entries.summary: <p>Less than a week after his second season as St. Viator coach ended, Bears great Robbie Gould has resigned.</p><p>In a release, the school said Gould "made the decision to step away from coaching to spend more time with his family."</p><p>The Lions missed the IHSA playoffs in both of Gould's years in charge, going 2-7 this year and 1-8 in 2025.</p><p>"We are grateful to Coach Gould for his leadership, dedication, and commitment to our student-athletes," St. Viator president Ryan Aiello said in the statement. "We appreciate his contributions to [St.] Viator football, respect his decision to prioritize his family and wish him all the best."</p><p>Gould took over at the Arlington Heights school after one season at Rolling Meadows. The Mustangs went 5-5 and lost to St. Charles North in the first round of the Class 7A playoffs.</p><p>Before moving into high school coaching, Gould played 18 seasons in the NFL — the first 11 with the Bears from 2005-15. He set the franchise career scoring record with 1.961 points and currently ranks 10th in NFL history. After leaving the Bears, he played one season for the Giants and six for the 49ers.</p><p>St. Viator, which plays its home games off campus, has announced plans for an on-campus stadium but the project has faced pushback from neighbors.<br>The school's statement said the search for a new coach has begun.</p>

entries.title: Victims in Mundelein murder-suicide shooting identified
entries.summary: <p>Mundelein police have released the identities of five people killed in an apparent murder-suicide this week.</p><p>Five adults, all related, were found dead after a concerned family member called for a well-being check in the 200 block of Wellington Street around 11:45 p.m. Sunday, Mundelein police said.</p><p>The Lake County Coroner's Office identified the deceased as 80-Year-old James Schmidt, 77-year-old Rebecca Schmidt, 22-year-old Maclaine Schmidt, 37-year-old Nicole Heiser and 51-year-old Bryan Schmidt. </p><p>Bryan Schmidt is believed to be the alleged perpetrator, police said.</p><p>He allegedly shot his four family members before turning the gun on himself, Mundelein police said the preliminary investigation found.</p><p>Multiple suicide notes were left by Bryan Schmidt and found on the scene, police said. The shootings are believed to have taken place between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. Sunday.</p><p>The family of Heiser, in a statement Wednesday, remembered the woman as a "bright, compassionate soul" who expressed deep love for animals and serving others. </p><p>"We refuse to let her be defined by this horrific violence or simply as a murder victim," the statement said. "Nicole was loyal beyond measure, generous in her time, and an esteemed animal empath — both professionally and within the community. Nicole had a great reverence for the natural world and lived with a sense of stewardship. We are so grateful for our beautiful time together and feel her presence strongly in our precious memories and calm winds."</p><p>Police said they have not had any prior contact with Bryan Schmidt and are working to determine the motive for the shooting.</p><p>Anyone with additional information on the incident is asked to call the Mundelein Police Department at 847-968-4600.</p>

entries.title: Foundry Park developers break ground on $3 billion project
entries.summary: <p>City and project officials broke ground Wednesday on Foundry Park, the $3 billion megadevelopment that promises to create a new neighborhood along the Chicago River’s North Branch — a vow that the land’s previous owner failed to keep after the pandemic.</p><p>Developer Jim Letchinger and Kayne Anderson Real Estate <a class="Link" 2025, after previous owner <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/06/27/lincoln-yards-sterling-bay-jdl-development-jim-letchinger-rahm-emanuel" >Sterling Bay</a> couldn’t follow through on its ambitious plans to build towering steel and glass buildings. </p><p>Letchinger’s real estate firm, JDL Development, is breaking ground on something more scaled back: a Capital is critical. We went through planning knowing that as soon as we get this done, we're building.”</p><p>Sterling Bay’s plans for the 53 acres of vacant land called for the equivalent of two Willis Towers’ worth of office space along the Chicago River between Bucktown and Lincoln Park — an amount that outpaced office demand after the COVID-19 pandemic.</p><p>The 31-acre Foundry Park is being built on the northern half of the former Lincoln Yards site and includes the old Finkl Steel property on Cortland Street, along the Chicago River.</p><p>“When I saw an opening to get involved in this incredible piece of land, I jumped at it,” Letchinger said. “Foundry Park offered a blank slate that would allow JDL to create another world-class neighborhood — and there's a lot of them in Chicago. This was an opportunity that we just could not miss.”</p><p>Plans call for more than 3,700 residences, with 20% of them affordable, and 970,000 square feet of office, retail and hotel space. Public parks, riverfront improvements and an extension of The 606 Trail are also planned.</p><p>Renderings show a mix of building heights, with the tallest at roughly 40 stories, grouped near open space and offering riverfront access. In another departure from Lincoln Yards, Foundry Park's buildings will be clad in traditional limestone and brick.</p><p>Phase one will include more than 725 residential units, retail, public green space and underground parking around Southport Avenue and Cortland and Kingsbury streets.</p><p>Letchinger is confident in the future success of Foundry Park because the mix of uses is flexible based on market demand. The homes will include rentals and for-purchase homes. Letchinger knows there’s an opportunity to build even more for-sale homes as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/08/01/cash-properties-sale-open-house-chicago-homebuyers-bidding-wars" >Chicago’s housing market</a> stays hot as inventory thins out.</p><p>“We know what people want,” Letchinger said. “We don't know if we can deliver all of the units right away, but we know over five, six, seven, eight years, the demand will be here. It's actually an unusual project where the more we build, the better it is because it's a neighborhood.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> entries.title: 2nd woman alleging sexual assault at a University of Chicago frat house feared she was drugged: police report
entries.summary: <p>A woman told Chicago police she feared she was drugged before being sexually assaulted at a University of Chicago fraternity house earlier this year, according to a police report.</p><p>On Feb. 8, a day after the assault reportedly happened, the 19-year-old told officers the alleged assailant gave her a shot of alcohol that “might have been laced,” the report says.</p><p>“The grief that this has imposed upon me is indescribable,” the woman <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/jane-doe-comes-forward-about-reported-rape-at-university-of-chicago-fraternity-ahead-of-public-safety-meeting/4005795/" target="_blank" >told NBC News</a>. “It is the first thing I think about whenever I wake up every day and the last thing I think about whenever I fall asleep.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/20/sexual-assault-university-of-chicago-uchicago-lawsuit" >The woman filed a lawsuit</a> Monday against the local and national Alpha Delta Phi organizations, alleging a member of the fraternity had assaulted “her limp body” during a party at the Alpha Delta Phi house, 5747 S. University Ave. The woman was identified only as “Jane Doe.”</p><p>The lawsuit came soon after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/13/university-of-chicago-sexual-assault-alpha-epsilon-pi" >another woman reported she was sexually assaulted</a> on Oct. 11 at an off-campus party at the Alpha Epsilon Pi house, located just a block away at 5625 S. University Ave. Witnesses in that case reported the accuser appeared “significantly more intoxicated than expected based on her reported alcohol consumption," according to another police report.</p><p>The two cases have placed the University of Chicago at the center of a national reckoning over sexual violence at colleges, sparked by reports of gang rape and drugging at a fraternity house at Cornell University in upstate New York. </p><p>The school's Public Safety Advisory Council, comprised of students, faculty, staff, and community members, discussed sexual misconduct on campus at a Wednesday night meeting. The council couldn't answer questions about the specific reported sexual assaults, but said it could make an official recommendation to the administration on how to address sexual assault on and near campus.</p><p>"This is literally the first time we've touched on this topic," said Sharon Fairley, a professor at the university's law school and chair of the council. "This is a learning process for us ... we're in the very early stages right now to see if this is a topic that is of such interest to the community where we feel like there may be a policy gap and we "These [cases] break my heart, because they're ... hard to prove because of timing," Spratt said.</p><p>The women alleging they were assaulted at the two fraternity houses aren’t students at the University of Chicago.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-dd0000" name="html-embed-module-dd0000"></a><div style="min-height:355px" id="datawrapper-vis-BBkuP"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BBkuP/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-BBkuP"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BBkuP/full.png" alt="Locator map" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The woman identified in her lawsuit as Jane Doe said she had two shots of alcohol at the Alpha Delta Phi house before meeting the alleged assailant, according to the police report. The suspect, identified in the lawsuit and the report as Kevin Shim, then gave Jane Doe another shot, after which she told police she “vaguely remembers anything,” the report says.</p><p>“I know myself, and that was not the amount with how intoxicated I felt after the shot that I took with him,” the woman told NBC News. “I’ve never felt like that before.”</p><p>In the lawsuit, she said she felt “unsteady and lightheaded” almost immediately after taking the drink. entries.title: DuPage County confirms measles case for vaccinated resident who traveled through O'Hare Airport
entries.summary: <p>A DuPage County resident with a confirmed case of measles traveled through O’Hare International Airport last week, health officials announced Wednesday.</p><p>The resident was vaccinated and returned from an international trip last Thursday, according to the DuPage County Health Department.</p><p>Health officials said it was “uncommon” for a vaccinated person to test positive for measles, but it was possible “when there is intense or prolonged exposure to a person with measles.”</p><p>“Our community’s safety is our priority,” said Adam Forker, executive director of the DCHD. “Our team is actively working on following up with individuals who may have been potentially exposed. Vaccination continues to provide strong protection, even in a rare breakthrough case.”</p><p>Health officials said they were working to contact anyone who may have been exposed.</p><p>Anyone who was at O'Hare Airport, Terminal 5 on Oct. 15 between 4:20 p.m. and 7:00 p.m. should contact DCHD at 630-682-7400.</p><p>As of Wednesday, there were 24 confirmed cases of measles so far this year, according to the Illinois Department of Public Health.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/09/10/2nd-measles-case-confirmed-in-kane-county" target="_blank" ><u>Last month</u></a>, health officials confirmed an out-of-state traveler with measles traveled through Union Station.</p><p>The stricken traveler was at Union Station on Aug. 27 after 8 p.m. through Aug. 28, according to a statement from the Chicago Department of Public Health.</p>

entries.title: Bulls add much-needed size with veteran Zach Collins finally returning
entries.summary: <p>It was an important night for Bulls veteran Zach Collins on Wednesday.</p><p>Simply because he played.</p><p>No small feat for the 6-foot-9 big, who had last played in an NBA game back on Dec. 27, 2025, before eventually undergoing season-ending surgery on his right toe. Just one of the injury issues that plagued Collins last year.</p><p>After a stellar start to his 2025 preseason, Collins fractured his left wrist and was lost until the start of December. He returned and was used as a double big in the Bulls’ lineup, doing so with some solid results. All Collins did in his 10 games was help the Bulls to a 6-4 record, averaging 9.7 points and 5.6 rebounds per game, but more importantly adding a physicality piece that the roster sorely lacked.</p><p>That’s why the new regime signed him to a two-year, $17-million deal on the first day of free agency, knowing he had injury issues.</p><p>He was slowed this preseason with a quad injury but finally came off the bench and got some run against Toronto. Call it easing Collins back into it with coach Tiago Splitter admitting the veteran was on a minutes restriction of 12-to-16 minutes for the time being.</p><p>“The tough part about Zach is he didn’t play yet,” Splitter said. “He didn’t play much last year, so we slowly want to put him there in the rotation and see those combinations, playing double-big or not. We’re going to have time to see it, have a small sample there, but we will try different combinations.”</p><p></p><p><b>King for a day</b></p><p></p><p>To further honor former Bulls broadcaster Stacey King in Wednesday’s opener, his broadcast partner Adam Amin wanted to call the first quarter by himself, leaving King’s chair empty. Robbie Hummel then joined the broadcast in the second quarter.</p><p>King died back in June after spending nearly 20 years as the color analyst for the Bulls.</p><p>The team also debuted their King patch that they will wear on their jerseys all season.</p><p></p><p><b>Rookie privilege?</b></p><p></p><p>Most NBA teams work the same when handling pregame shooting order during warmups. The veterans go last, while the rookies and deep bench guys get their work in early.</p><p>So it was a bit strange in the preseason that the Bulls’ Caleb Wilson was not only in the final group, but at home games even gets his own music played, usually the lyrics of Chicago rapper Lucki.</p><p>If this was some No. 4 overall pick flexing his muscle to get special treatment, however, Wilson put that to rest.</p><p>“Honestly, I don’t know how that happened, being in the last (pregame shooting) slot,” Wilson said. “I just told them give me whatever was available and then the (United Center) DJ, he’s cool, got the mohawk. I met him when we did media day and he knew my favorite artist was Lucki, so every time I come out, he plays him for me.”</p><p>And just to make sure Wilson was reminded he is still a rookie? Veteran Norman Powell made all the young guys use pink “Hello Kitty” luggage for the trip to Toronto.</p><p></p><p><b>Staying put</b></p><p></p><p>The traveling party was a bit thinner for this two-game road trip with rookie Dailyn Swain and guard Jordan Hawkins staying back in Chicago to deal with illness.</p><p>The Bulls play the Bucks on Friday so both players could possibly join the team in Milwaukee, but Splitter wasn’t going to force the issue, especially since Swain and Hawkins were on the outside looking in as far as the rotation.</p>

entries.title: Bulls get thumped in season debut as rebuild looks like demolition site
entries.summary: <p>A Norman Powell missed floater, a Josh Giddey errant pass, and then a welcome-to-the-Association moment when rookie Caleb Wilson was stripped by a player he idolized growing up in Kawhi Leonard.</p><p>All just 90 seconds into Wednesday’s Bulls season opener, transforming a perceived rebuild into something that resembled more like a demolition site.</p><p>And just like that Bulls basketball debuted to a resounding thud.</p><p>Was the 135-92 trouncing – the worst loss in a season opener in Bulls history – unexpected? Not really. But with all the excitement around the team – whether it was the high-flying No. 4 pick in Wilson, new coach Tiago Splitter or just the gloomy clouds that seemed to leave with the arrival of the new front office, it was supposed to feel a lot better than it looked.</p><p>A reminder of the reality of the NBA: Good feelings only last so long because at some point the game has to be played.</p><p>Maybe that’s why Splitter called a timeout just 90 seconds into the game, as he saw his young team down 7-0 and drowning.</p><p>A life preserver that only kept his team afloat for so long.</p><p>“The way we competed,” Splitter said of what bothered him most about that start. “After a turnover, getting our heads down when running back, that’s something we cannot accept. Talked to them at halftime, after the game, we gotta be better.”</p><p>It seemingly can’t get worse.</p><p>Through most of the game, the deficit was in the 30ss, even reaching as much as 48 points. An Eastern Conference contender against a team that will be fighting to stay out of the bottom three of the league all season long on full display.</p><p>Also on display?</p><p>An All-Star frontcourt in Leonard and Scottie Barnes against two youngsters in Wilson and Matas Buzelis. Men dealing with boys.</p><p>No wonder Splitter was concerned with the matchup. Not just in the frontcourt but the entire roster, especially on the defensive end where there weren’t a lot of answers.</p><p>“We knew they had guys that can steal the ball, and we knew a lot about their physicality,” Splitter said. “Sometimes you gotta feel it and know it when you go there and play.”</p><p>Wilson did just that, finishing with 16 points, but doing so on a 7-of-21 shooting night with nine turnovers and a minus-45 in plus/minus.</p><p>“Obviously it was a bad night for Caleb,” Splitter said. “We’re going to grow from this, learn from this. He was playing too much in crowds, not passing the ball when he had two, three guys on him, so we’re going to watch film and get better.”</p><p>Considering the Bulls (0-1) finished 27-of-85 (32%) from the field and 4-of-36 (11%) from three, while allowing the Raptors to shoot 44-of-98 (45%) and turn them over 27 times, getting better should be a low bar.</p><p>Wilson agreed with Splitter that he had to experience an NBA game as the ultimate teacher.</p><p>“I just got to figure it out,” Wilson said. “That’s the great thing about the NBA is we play 82 games, so able to watch film, my coaches tell me things I can do better, so it’s about going out there and doing it. Flim is a great way to see where you should be and could be, but you just got to go out there and do it.”</p><p>They’ll have a practice in Toronto on Thursday to do just that before taking on Milwaukee in an afternoon tilt on Friday.</p><p>“Yes, I’m worried about that,” Splitter responded when asked about making sure his team doesn’t fall into bad habits. “We got to get better.”</p>

entries.title: Charges pending after hours-long SWAT standoff on Far South Side
entries.summary: <p>Charges were pending for a man with a gun who holed himself up inside a Far South Side home for five hours and fired a shot Wednesday night.</p><p>Officers conducted a well-being check around 8:05 p.m. in the 13300 block of South Michigan Avenue after receiving a 911 call that a "known" man barricaded himself inside a home with the caller's firearm, Chicago police said. </p><p>While inside, the man discharged the firearm, though no one was struck, police said. </p><p>Shortly after 1 a.m., he was taken into custody without incident and also taken to a hospital to be evaluated, police said. </p><p>Charges were pending.</p>

entries.title: Rulings on traffic stop, child custody case uphold civil rights
entries.summary: <p>Since 1871, a <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/1983" target="_blank" >federal statute</a> has authorized Americans to sue state and local officials for violating their constitutional rights. But since 1982, thanks to the <a class="Link" href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/457/800/" target="_blank" >court-invented</a> doctrine of <a class="Link" href="https://ij.org/report/unaccountable/the-controversy-over-qualified-immunity/" target="_blank" >qualified immunity</a>, such claims have been allowed only when they allege violations of "clearly established" law.</p><p>Because courts often require plaintiffs to meet that standard by citing precedents involving closely similar facts, qualified immunity can prove insurmountable even for victims of <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2022/01/21/glenn-youngkin-qualified-immunity-nothing-conservative-about-letting-police-violate-our-rights/" target="_blank" >outrageous abuses</a>. But as two recent cases illustrate, there are limits to this license for misconduct, meaning officials may still be held accountable when they flout long-standing constitutional principles, even when they do so in novel ways.</p><p>In 2022, Mario Rosales and Gracie Lasyone <a class="Link" href="https://ij.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/LA-Rosales-Traffic-Stop-Complaint.pdf" target="_blank" >sued</a> two Alexandria, Louisiana, police officers, Samuel Terrell and Jim Lewis, alleging that they had pulled Rosales over without legal justification. The cops ordered Rosales and Lasyone, his girlfriend, out of the car and detained them for 21 minutes, during which they grilled the couple about illegal drugs, frisked Rosales and instructed him to empty his pockets.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-320000" name="module-320000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Terrell and Lewis sought refuge in qualified immunity. But last month, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/09/28/the-5th-circuit-rejects-qualified-immunity-for-cops-who-searched-a-driver-after-a-bogus-traffic-stop/" target="_blank" >ruled</a> that Rosales and Lasyone had plausibly alleged several Fourth Amendment violations, including a stop based on a "fabricated traffic violation," an improperly prolonged detention and unjustified searches.</p><p>In reaching that conclusion, the 5th Circuit relied mainly on a 1968 <a class="Link" href="https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-392/pdf/USREPORTS-392-1.pdf" target="_blank" >decision</a> in which the Supreme Court said police may detain someone only if they reasonably suspect he is involved in criminal activity and may frisk him only if they reasonably suspect he is "armed and dangerous." Assuming the facts alleged in the lawsuit are true, the three-judge panel unanimously <a class="Link" href="https://cases.justia.com/federal/appellate-courts/ca5/25-30650/25-30650-2026-09-22.pdf" target="_blank" >held</a>, Terrell and Lewis had failed both of those tests.</p><p>When the officers stopped Rosales, the principles that the 5th Circuit applied had been the law of the land for more than half a century. Terrell and Lewis nevertheless argued that "any constitutional violation arising from the traffic stop was not clearly established," which gives you a sense of the chutzpah that qualified immunity invites.</p><p>Police commonly <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2020/05/17/10-ways-a-roadside-police-stop-can-go-wrong/" target="_blank" >pull drivers over</a>, ostensibly for traffic violations, in the hope of implicating them in drug crimes. A case that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/10/15/the-8th-circuit-rejects-qualified-immunity-for-a-judge-who-jailed-2-kids-for-refusing-to-follow-directions/" target="_blank" >considered</a> this month involved a much more unusual scenario: a judge who locked two children in jail cells because he was frustrated by their resistance to a parental custody decision.</p><p>During a 2019 hearing in Taney County, Missouri, a divorced couple agreed that the mother would have primary custody of their two children, then 12 and 14. But contrary to that agreement, the children did not want to go home with their mother, which led to an argument in the courthouse lobby.</p><p>Judge Eric Eighmy intervened, telling the children they had to leave with their mother and repeatedly warning them that they could end up in foster care if they refused to do so. When that did not work, Eighmy jailed them until they became more cooperative.</p><p>"The time spent in the holding-cell area was between twenty and forty minutes," the 8th Circuit noted. And since Eighmy did not have probable cause to believe the children had committed any offense, "much less one that justified placing them in a holding cell," the court said, their confinement clearly violated the Fourth Amendment.</p><p>If so, Eighmy argued, he had no way of knowing that. The 8th Circuit panel unanimously disagreed: "As we put it over a decade and a half ago, long before the events in this case, 'it is clearly established that a warrantless arrest, unsupported by probable cause, violates the Fourth Amendment.'"</p><p>Notably, the 8th Circuit did not think the bizarre details of the case counted in Eighmy's favor.</p><p>"We are not concerned about the lack of a prior case" with "fundamentally similar" facts, it said. "Indeed, given how clear the law is, it would have been surprising to find one."</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f40000" name="module-f40000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Early voting numbers ominous for Republicans
entries.summary: <p>It’s true every election year, but this cycle especially: It’s the economy, stupid.</p><p>Voters have told us in nearly every poll and interview that they are deeply concerned about affordability and the rising cost of goods, from gas to groceries.</p><p>That doesn’t bode well for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party, as we also know most voters blame them for inflation and the economic hardships caused by Trump’s tariffs and Iran war.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-580000" name="module-580000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Also like every other election, this one will come down to turnout. And if we can make some assumptions about early voting and voter registration, that doesn’t bode well for Republicans either.</p><p>In states all over the country, including where we’re watching hotly contested Senate races, voters are smashing early voting records — which means they’re more motivated and enthusiastic than ever before in a midterm cycle.</p><p>While we don’t know who, exactly, these early voters are, it’s hard to imagine that in this environment, with the president’s approval numbers in the gutter, with the economy in such a terrible state, and with no end to the Iran war in sight, that these people are running out to the polls to vote for … two more years of this.</p><p>One presumes, to the contrary, that many of these voters feel enraged, betrayed and embarrassed by what they’ve witnessed these last two years — the chaos, the rank corruption, the naked self-dealing, the broken promises, and a president who seems focused on all the wrong things.</p><p>If you’re a farmer in Iowa, for example, whose diesel prices have skyrocketed 80% since last year, or if you’re a mom in Pennsylvania, which has seen the highest year-over-year inflation, it’s doubtful you’re eager to double down on Trump’s agenda of ballrooms and crypto.</p><p>And there’s some data to back up the hunch.</p><p>Per a <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/01/politics/cnn-early-voting-takeaways-democratic-advantage" target="_blank" >CNN report</a>, in several states with key Senate or governor races, Dems are making up a larger share of voters requesting ballots than they did in 2024.</p><p>In Iowa, where Republican Ashley Hinson is neck and neck with her Democratic challenger Josh Turek in a tight Senate race, Dems have made 67% of the ballot requests, up 13 points from this time in 2024.</p><p>Ballot requests are also up among Dems in Pennsylvania, Maine and North Carolina.</p><p>In <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/11/politics/early-voting-midterms-ohio-democratic-shift-vis" target="_blank" >Ohio</a>, where Democrat Sherrod Brown and Republican Jon Husted are in a close race for Senate, affiliated Dem voters make up a larger share of early voters than they did last cycle, and even in the most Republican counties.</p><p>In the first four days of early voting in <a class="Link" href="https://www.firstcoastnews.com/article/news/politics/elections/early-voting-questions-election-georgia/77-823e17f1-5e31-43f2-b01e-84c078663cfb" target="_blank" >Georgia</a>, more than 600,000 ballots were cast, breaking previous records.</p><p>Voter registration in <a class="Link" href="https://www.texastribune.org/2026/10/16/texas-voter-registration-2026-election/" target="_blank" >Texas</a>, where James Talarico is threatening to become the first Democrat to win a Senate race there in 38 years, reached a record 19 million, up nearly 8% since 2022.</p><p>Even in states that aren’t fielding competitive races, voters seem unusually motivated. In <a class="Link" href="https://rhodeislandcurrent.com/2026/09/08/early-in-person-voting-breaks-rhode-island-record/" target="_blank" >Rhode Island</a>, early voting has doubled since 2022 and tripled since 2024.</p><p>In <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbc4i.com/news/u-s-world/early-voting-surges-across-key-battleground-states-ahead-of-midterms/" target="_blank" >Virginia</a>, early voting has doubled since 2022.</p><p>More than <a class="Link" href="https://spectrumlocalnews.com/us/snplus/politics/2026/10/14/early-voting-midterm-elections" target="_blank" >4 million</a> Americans have already cast their ballots, and that isn’t good news for Republicans, who have been drowning in a sea of bad news and bad polls for the last month.</p><p>Sure, some Republicans may be holding their votes until Election Day, coaxed by Trump in previous cycles not to vote early or by mail. But Republican candidates, who are having to spend exorbitant amounts of money to compete in places they haven’t in decades, in some cases, have to hope they can turn out every last base voter in friendly corners.</p><p>And they have to hope this early enthusiasm cuts for them too.</p><p>But with a president who seems hellbent on destroying the economy — and Republicans’ chances of keeping the majority, it’s hard to imagine who would be excited to vote for more of this.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-0c0000" name="module-0c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: Dear Abby: Guys agreed to bachelor party trip, then heard the price and backed out
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I helped plan a 12-guy bachelor party in Boston. The best man's initial email outlined the itinerary — two nights away and a Bruins game — and included a link to the Airbnb. Everyone RSVP'd with an enthusiastic "yes." With headcounts locked, we booked the lodging and group-rate tickets. The total came to $565 per person (including covering the bachelor).</p><p>Once the price was announced, three guys backed out. I offered installment plans, but they refused. We filled one spot but were still left holding a huge deficit. While on the trip, the remaining attendees agreed that the dropouts should help cover the nonrefundable losses. We asked them for a reduced fee of $200 each. One of them paid, one sent half and the third has gone silent. They are all furious. I understand money is tight, but they shouldn't have committed before we pulled the trigger on bookings. Are we wrong for asking them to pay for backing out late? — <i>STUCK WITH THE BILL</i></p><p><b>DEAR STUCK:</b> Airbnb and traditional hotels ask for a booking deposit so that they won't lose money if someone backs out of a reservation. You should have done the same. If you had collected some or all of the money for the trip before making the deposit, you wouldn't have suffered such a big loss when people changed their minds.</p><p>Because there is fault on both sides, $200 seems like a reasonable compromise to me. Thank the man who paid the full requested amount. I wouldn't pressure the others or ever mention it again — even if they choose not to pay. They're probably embarrassed that they couldn't afford to join in, and as the saying goes, "You can't squeeze blood from a stone."</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My granddaughter, "Melanie," hates me. She is 11 and a pre-teen, but she has been like this for many years. I don't know why. Melanie won't even say hello to me when I greet her. She'll let me take her and her friends to places that cost lots of money, but she doesn't want to be with me. She's hateful, and I correct her sometimes, but her parents never correct her when she does it. Melanie never, ever says thank you when I do something for her and never lets me touch her. Should I give up and wait to see if she will come back to me? — <i>MISSING HOW IT COULD BE</i></p><p><b>DEAR MISSING:</b> The fault for your granddaughter's misbehavior lies with her parents, who should have taught her common courtesy and respect for others. Rather than give up, take a step back. Quit rewarding her bad behavior. Shut your wallet, stop buying her gifts, and stop taking her and her friends places. Do not try to touch her.</p><p>When you see her at family gatherings smile, say "Hello, Melanie, how are you?" When she ignores you, concentrate on the other relatives and let yourself have a good time. Melanie may or may not grow out of her bratty stage, but you are being foolish to let it affect you.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Time is an ingredient in Sen Morimoto’s fourth studio album
entries.summary: <p>Growing up in rural Wendell, Massachusetts, Sen Morimoto found a rust-ridden abandoned car deep in the woods behind their parents’ house. Two decades later, the car was still there — though its origin still remains a mystery to Morimoto, now 32. It takes center stage in the music video for “Overthinker,” the lead single off their new time-bending album out Friday.</p><p>“As a kid, it was something that really fascinated me because there’s no roads,” the artist explained. “How did this car get into the middle of the woods?”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/7JdZpXsx7eU?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Sen Morimoto - Overthinker (Official Music Video)"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Morimoto collapses past and present on their new album, “Time Is On Your Side,” reflecting on the 13 years since they moved from Massachusetts to Chicago. In that time the Japanese-American musician has released three studio albums, found a firm footing in Chicago’s independent music community and, in 2018, became co-owner of local indie label Sooper Records, which celebrated its 10th anniversary earlier this year.</p><p>“Time Is On Your Side” is Morimoto’s first public release in nearly three years; the artist took a break from releasing new music after their industry-critiquing album “Diagnosis” in 2023, but noted they’re constantly making music all the while.</p><p>“I’ve had a lot of friends tell me they’re surprised I’m putting out music again,” they said. “I didn’t realize maybe I was giving off such a vibe that I had totally quit.”</p><p>A few months into the break, Morimoto got back into the studio with collaborator Brok Mende, audio engineer at Friends of Friends Recording in Humboldt Park, armed with a general idea of working on a new project and no timetable.</p><p>“That was sort of the goal from the beginning of it, to force time into the equation,” Morimoto said, adding, “by not allowing the pressure of being in the studio to make you act quickly and skip over some of the details. entries.title: This Illinois law was supposed to help families. It’s failing them instead.
entries.summary: <p>After a traumatic week of labor with their first child that ended in a cesarean section, Eleanor Grano and her husband were burned out.</p><p>They got home from the hospital after the major abdominal surgery with their newborn son, and with the help of family paid about $2,400 for a doula to care for their baby overnight for nearly a week. This allowed Grano and her husband E.J. Fagan to rest and recover. Their parents and siblings don’t live nearby.</p><p>Grano and Fagan say their experience was transformative. Having a doula watch over their baby boy as they slept brought Grano relief and gave her time to care for herself. They call him Cinco, the fifth Edward in the family.</p><p>Then the doula’s time was up. Grano struggled with postpartum anxiety and grew exhausted from the around-the-clock care. She feared Cinco would die in his sleep.</p><p>“It was just this forever, all-consuming experience for me that … after I’ve gone through three years of infertility, miscarriage, like all the battle wounds of infertility, that I was somehow still at risk of losing my child,” Grano recalls of her first baby born two years ago.</p><p>So as she and Fagan, of west suburban Riverside, thought about having another baby, they planned the pregnancy around a <a class="Link" href="https://gov-pritzker-newsroom.prezly.com/gov-pritzker-signs-birth-equity-legislation" target="_blank" ><u>new Illinois law</u></a>. It is intended to cover roughly a month of doula visits, capped at $8,000. Grano called it a lifeboat.</p><p>In 2024, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/07/29/pritzker-signing-ceremony-legislation-expansion-abortion-coverage-black-maternal-deaths" target="_blank" ><u>Gov. JB Pritzker signed</u></a> the Birth Equity Initiative to help prevent more women from dying, especially women of color. One key part of the law is broadening access to doulas.</p><p>Doulas are trained professionals who support families. They advocate on behalf of women in the delivery room and help manage pain, or take care of newborns in the first weeks of their lives.</p><p>People with private insurance, like Grano and Fagan, could have a doula with <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/ilcs/fulltext?DocName=021500050K356z.40" target="_blank" ><u>no cost sharing</u></a>. The message to families: You won’t have to pay.</p><p>“Illinois has been the wild west of insurance companies,” Democrat state Rep. Robyn Gabel, a lead sponsor of the legislation, said at a news conference the day Pritzker signed the law. “They have pretty much done whatever they wanted, and in this administration, that is not going to be true any longer.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-8f0000" name="image-8f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f067e99/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F00%2F2a%2F5028f27440c79037cc79a6943aff%2Fpritzkersigning-073024-24.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dc6dae3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F00%2F2a%2F5028f27440c79037cc79a6943aff%2Fpritzkersigning-073024-24.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b98c265/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F00%2F2a%2F5028f27440c79037cc79a6943aff%2Fpritzkersigning-073024-24.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Gov. JB Pritzker sits at a table and signs the Birth Equity Initiative law at Chicago Beyond in West Loop on July 29, 2024. Beside him is Lt. Gov. JB Pritzker signed the Birth Equity Initiative law in July 2024. To his right is Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton, who spearheaded the law. At the time, she said that the law ensures that when families grow “both mom and baby have access to care they need to get home safely.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Standing nearby was Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton, who <a class="Link" href="https://www.julianastratton.com/meet-juliana" target="_blank" ><u>led the push</u></a> for the law, which was part of a broader plan to invest in birth centers to diapers, an expense that can drain a family budget. She’s called it a <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/ltgovstratton/photos/the-birth-equity-initiative-is-a-national-blueprint-for-saving-the-lives-of-preg/1124924859448847/" target="_blank" ><u>national blueprint</u></a> for saving the lives of pregnant women. It’s <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2026/04/06/lt-gov-juliana-stratton-her-us-senate-campaign-health-care-funding-and-raising-minimum" target="_blank" ><u>part of her campaign</u></a> for U.S. Senate this fall.</p><p>But passing a law is one thing. Implementing it is another.</p><p>Private insurers were supposed to be ready to cover doulas on Jan. 1, but the law is still missing key pieces. Families are paying the price, according to a WBEZ investigation.</p><p>And only an estimated 30% of people with private insurance in Illinois have plans the state can regulate. For everyone else, it could be much harder to access this benefit.</p><p>Grano is due this week with a baby girl. She has spent nearly her entire pregnancy fighting her insurer, Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Illinois, the dominant insurer in the state, to cover her postpartum doula. Hours of messaging with various Blue Cross representatives. Lots of stress during her high-risk pregnancy, Grano says. The insurer wanted her to cover the cost — around $10,000 — then seek reimbursement later, a huge financial risk.</p><p>In another case, a Chicago couple who had their baby girl about five months ago, is still trying to get Blue Cross to fully reimburse them for their overnight doula. And the insurer is trying to claw back nearly $2,000 it already paid, according to records the family shared with WBEZ.</p><p>The roadblocks to families when they need support the most, for a benefit they’re legally entitled to, are happening across the region. In many cases, doula agencies say women stop trying to use insurance to pay for support because it’s so much work.</p><p>“The families that we know are often limited on resources are the ones that really need the doula support, and they’re not getting it,” says Anna Rodney, who owns Chicago Family Doulas, a large organization that works with more than 500 doulas.</p><p>Presented with WBEZ’s findings, Gabel says she plans to advance a bill that would fix a major shortcoming with the law.</p><p>“If a family is interested in having a doula, they should be able to have one,” she tells WBEZ.</p><h3>Trying to prevent a crisis </h3><p>Doulas are becoming <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2024/12/03/cook-county-is-launching-a-free-doula-program-for-pregnant-patients" target="_blank" ><u>more mainstream</u></a> as doctors and governments try to address an alarming inequity.</p><p>In Illinois, <a class="Link" href="https://dph.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/idph/publications/idph/topics-and-services/life-stages-populations/maternal-child-family-health-services/maternal-health/maternal-mortality-data-report-2025.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>Black women are three times</u></a> as likely to die from a pregnancy-related medical condition compared to white women. One in 3 women die more than 60 days after giving birth, regardless of race.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10292163/" target="_blank" ><u>Research shows</u></a> having a doula is linked to better health outcomes for mothers and babies, including fewer premature births and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/environment-public-health/2024/05/11/endeavor-health-study-targets-c-section-rates-black-maternal-health" target="_blank" ><u>lower C-section rates</u></a>.</p><p>Pritzker started doula coverage for families with low incomes or disabilities in the state’s Medicaid health insurance program about two years ago, <a class="Link" href="https://healthlaw.org/doulamedicaidproject/map/?state=IL&tab=current-coverage-landscape" target="_blank" ><u>joining nearly 30 other states.</u></a></p><div class="Enhancement" Fagan calls what his insurer, Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Illinois, is doing “malicious compliance.” He’s an associate professor of political science at the University of Illinois Chicago and uses his wife’s advocacy as an example to students.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Too good to be true</h3><p>Grano’s experience isn’t isolated. So many calls pour in to Chicago Family Doulas when the doula benefit starts this year that Rodney, its owner, hires an extra employee to answer them. But most of the time, families can’t get straight answers from their insurers and can’t afford a doula otherwise, she says.</p><p>“Every once in a while I see that somebody got coverage, and I’m like, “Oh my gosh, that’s insane,” Rodney says. “We’ll ask them, ‘What did you do?’ But I almost think it’s like a fluke or working really, really hard resubmitting, resubmitting.”</p><p>She mentions a rare success story of sorts: Katie Lombardi and her husband Louis Massard. Their daughter Clara was born in May, joining big sister Elia, who is 3.</p><p>Lombardi verifies with their insurer, Blue Cross, multiple times that they are eligible for a postpartum doula, she tells WBEZ. Customer service representatives never mention having to use a doula in-network, she says.</p><p>“The whole thing honestly seemed too good to be true,” says Lombardi, who lives in Andersonville on the North Side.</p><p>They hire a doula who tends to Clara overnight — feeding and swaddling her, washing bottles, folding laundry — as the family tries to get their older kiddo to sleep and to rest themselves. She comes twice, then Lombardi and Massard hit pause in a moment of panic after Blue Cross indicates they won’t cover it.</p><p>Then a check arrives in the mail reimbursing them. So they decide to try again and hire another overnight doula, who comes around twice a week for a few weeks. Their total cost out of pocket: about $4,500.</p><p>Again, Massard submits claims to Blue Cross. Some are fully paid. Others are not. It doesn’t make sense why, he says.</p><p>“This just reinforces why so many people don’t trust insurance companies,” Lombardi says. “You feel like insurance companies are almost never making decisions that are in the interest of their real customers, people like us on the other side of it.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a70000" name="image-a70000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8a5a54d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F49%2F405affcc4ca681c95bb89d8521af%2Fdoulalaw-260927-004.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c385840/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F49%2F405affcc4ca681c95bb89d8521af%2Fdoulalaw-260927-004.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/aec75c9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F49%2F405affcc4ca681c95bb89d8521af%2Fdoulalaw-260927-004.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Eleanor Grano stands on the back porch of her Riverside home on Sept. 15, 2026. A new state law requires private insurers cover the cost of doulas. But Grano learned she’d have to pay up front and then ask for reimbursement. The cost: around $10,000 for a month of overnight stays. Grano and her husband feared they would never get paid back.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Like Grano, Massard spends hours going back and forth with Blue Cross, navigating an alphabet soup of billing codes and receipts. He includes detailed cover sheets to help Blue Cross understand the claims he submits. Four claims have been reimbursed so far after a cycle of angry calls and messages, he explains.</p><p>Blue Cross still owes them about $1,800 and is trying to claw back around $1,800 it already reimbursed, Massard says.</p><p>He’s an attorney and writes an appeal to Blue Cross citing the Birth Equity Initiative and asking for an explanation of why the same claims for the same services are being treated differently.</p><p>“The best you can hope for after a contentious phone call with them is that the status online will change the following day, and then maybe maybe a week later they might issue a check — or they might issue a check and then a week later ask for their money back,” Massard says.</p><p>Ament declined to discuss Lombardi and Massard’s experience.</p><h3>‘There is no meaningful oversight’</h3><p>One of the reasons some families can’t get doulas paid for is because the majority of people in Illinois with private insurance have plans the state can't regulate, according to the Illinois Department of Insurance. For these families, their insurers aren’t required by the state to cover doulas, though they can, says Caron Brookens, a spokesperson for the state insurance department.</p><p>What’s more, for people whose insurers are required by the Birth Equity Initiative to cover doula services, legislators left a key part out of the law. They did not create a standard for how many doulas insurers must have in their networks or how far people have to travel to access one, Brookens confirms.</p><p>Insurers must meet what’s called a “network adequacy” standard for other types of providers in their networks, from pediatricians to orthopedic surgeons. Without one for doulas, insurers can decide how many they contract with as part of their networks.</p><p>If it’s a small pool, families might have to do what Grano and Lombardi did: find an out-of-network doula, pay them if they can, then try to get reimbursed by their insurer.</p><p>It’s confusing for families who see politicians tout the benefit of the Birth Equity Initiative: no cost-sharing.</p><p>Without a standard for doulas, insurers don’t have to tell state insurance regulators how many are in their networks. They also don’t have to say how much in claims they’ve paid for doula services, the department responded to a WBEZ public records request. That makes it hard to know if and where there are gaps in access.</p><p>“The implementation of the law on … private insurance has been lacking, and on private insurance I think there is no meaningful oversight,” says Kathy Waligora, deputy director of external affairs at EverThrive Illinois, a statewide advocacy group for maternal and child health. “It’s not clear that there are enough doulas to have an adequate network, but you could start trying. Robyn Gabel, a lead sponsor of the Birth Equity Initiative, says she plans to advance a bill in January that would fix a major shortcoming in the law.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Gabel, a lead sponsor of the law, says the bill she plans to file in January would require network adequacy for doulas.</p><p>“There needs to be a little more pressure to make sure that the insurance companies recruit doulas and make sure that they have doulas in their networks,” Gabel says.</p><p>Ann Gillespie, director of the state insurance department, declined an on-the-record interview. The department is charged with implementing and enforcing the law.</p><p>Stratton, who spearheaded the law, also declined an interview request.</p><p>In response to questions, Brookens says the department can investigate complaints and encourages families and providers to file them. The state also audits insurers to see if they violate the law. But any violations for doula coverage likely won't be reported until 2027 or 2028 because the state typically reviews at least a full year of records, and the doula benefit for private insurance is new.</p><p>Grano’s complaint is one of a few related to doula services filed with the state. The department would not provide them, citing confidentiality.</p><p>Rodney says it’s a big ask for her more than 500 doulas to apply to join insurance networks. They’re independent contractors, not employees. It’s a cumbersome and time-consuming process.</p><p>And she wonders how much insurers would reimburse her doulas and how long it would take them to get paid. Some live paycheck to paycheck.</p><p>Insurers taking weeks, even months to pay providers is a <a class="Link" href="https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/billions-in-profits-millions-in-unpaid-claims-medicaid-insurers-leave-illinois-providers-struggling-patients-losing-care/" target="_blank" ><u>common complaint</u></a>. Now Rodney pays her doulas weekly after they work with families.</p><h3>Blue Cross relents </h3><p>After WBEZ reached out to Blue Cross this fall about Grano’s experience, the insurer expedited her case and added her doula to its network. She and Fagan no longer have to pay $10,000 up front and risk not getting paid back.</p><p>Now they have 16 visits with a postpartum doula, half as many as Blue Cross originally said. This is a potential limit laid out in the law.</p><p>“Am I still worried that they’re not going to pay up? entries.title: Greg McCarty, beloved parking garage attendant at lakefront condo building, dies at 74
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Greg McCarty had a superpower.</p><p>Residents at 3900 N. Lake Shore Drive, the condo building where Mr. McCarty worked for 48 years as a parking attendant, knew it well.</p><p>He made people feel special.</p><p>A typical garage interaction unfolded one recent morning when Mr. McCarty saw resident Lauren Sauer and announced "Hey, just so you know." </p><p>He then broke into the Stevie Wonder song "I Just Called to Say I Love You."</p><p>Sauer, a real estate agent and former professional singer, took the cue.</p><p>"He loved to sing — could be Stevie or anything, really — and he and I would harmonize together in the garage," Sauer said.</p><p>He had this power to make people feel special," Sauer said."I've never met anyone like him before."</p><p>Broad, over six feet tall, and possessing an easy smile, Mr. McCarty performed duties far beyond parking and retrieving cars.</p><p>He helped with groceries, held doors, washed cars, filled tires that needed air, fixed home appliances and identified any car issues and suggested reputable cars mechanics.</p><p>"He never was looking for a tip," said Doug Silverstein, a resident and former hospital administrator. "He’d be embarrassed if you ever tried to give him money."</p><p>During quiet times in the garage, he sometimes drew flowers with colored pencils and gifted his creations to building residents.</p><p>"I have one on my fridge," Sauer said. "It's funny you don't think of a garage valet as someone who's going to become a key person in your daily life, but he truly was a wonderful guy." </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div </div> </div><p>Mr. McCarty died Aug. 18 after suffering a heart attack. He was 74.</p><p>"Everybody in the building seemed to have a relationship with Greg," said Bill Wheelhouse, former state capitol bureau chief for Illinois Public Radio in Springfield. "Mine just started talking sports and basketball, and I wasn't even that big of a basketball fan."</p><p>Wheelhouse got skybox tickets to a Chicago Bulls game and invited Mr. McCarty.</p><p>"He was really kind of one of my first acquaintances and friends when we moved to Chicago a few years ago," said Wheelhouse, whose wife, in tribute, put flowers on the ledge of a flowerbed outside the building where Mr. McCarty sat during the quiet moments of his shift.</p><p>Soon more flowers and balloons were left there, too.</p><p>"We're going to have a memorial plaque put at that spot to honor him, with a little ceremony to unveil it in January," said Luther Goins, a theater producer and director who lives in the building.</p><p>"He made all of us feel that life was a little better for meeting a guy like this," said Goins. "And he was a stunning example of someone who was committed to his job."</p><p>Mr. McCarty, who grew up in a small town in Mississippi and in Chicago, lived in South Shore with his wife, Evadney McCarty.</p><p>"They met when they lived in the same building and she asked him to fix a light bulb because he was tall," said Mr. McCarty's nephew, Fabian Higgins.</p><p>"He was very old school, didn't have a credit card or any debt, took great care of the things in his life, like his Eddie Bauer-edition Ford Explorer, which had more than 300,000 miles on it when it finally died out this summer," Higgins said.</p><p>"And he was very loyal and committed, especially to his wife, he loved her and did a lot for her," Higgins said.</p><p>As a kid, he was in a singing group that loved to perform songs by The Temptations, his family said.</p><p>More than a dozen building residents attended Mr. McCarty's funeral, and more than 100 wrote cards to his family.</p><p>"Greg was a gentle giant," said his sister, Sherrie Gamblin. </p><p>"What you see is what you get with Greg, and I love him like a brother," said Henry L. James, a colleague who has worked as a parking attendant at the building for nearly as long as Mr. McCarty.</p><p>Mr. McCarty is survived by his wife, Evadney McCarty, and his sisters, Betty Forbes and Sherrie Gamblin.</p><p>Services have been held.</p>

entries.title: Giant puppets and dozens of dancers will fuel Chicago’s Arts in the Dark Parade
entries.summary: <p>As the sun sets on Saturday night, Chicago's Columbus Drive will come alive with a fire-breathing dragon, giant animal puppets, and scores of drumlines and dance troupes.  </p><p>The annual Arts in the Dark parade, now in its 12th year, is not your typical parade. entries.title: Griffin MSI defends its criticized Welcome Hall design
entries.summary: <p>The Griffin Museum of Science and Industry contemplated seven glassy and visually transparent Welcome Hall designs before selecting the one now criticized as too big and obstructive for the landmark site.</p><p>"I think there was a little bit of tension — a healthy tension — between it being just sort of the Apple Store glass monument and this beautiful Charles Atwood historic neoclassical building, or something that had some commonality [with the museum]," RAMSA Associate Partner Caitlin Getman, the project's lead designer, said.</p><p>Getman said the chosen design achieves "compatibility that ... clearly distinguishes itself as different" from the museum building.</p><p>The schemes were shown to me during an exclusive 90-minute interview Monday with Griffin MSI CEO Chevy Humphrey, Getman and the project's preservation consultant Emily Ramsey.</p><p>The museum wouldn't make the seven renderings available for publication, though. A spokesperson said the renderings were "early drafts" that showed "all the evolution that’s happened."</p><p>But during our talk, Humphrey, Getman and Ramsey shared new images and diagrams of the Welcome Hall planned for the front lawn of the museum's 57th Street main entrance.</p><p>They said the hall, which would link to the museum by way of a glass connection through the middle of the building’s exterior front stairs, would architecturally enhance the 133-year-old Greek Revival beauty.</p><p>They also said the 28-foot tall, 458-foot wide hall would provide admission-free public spaces, with galleries and restrooms, and make it easier for the museum's 1.5 million yearly visitors to enter the building.</p><p>"There needs to be free spaces and places where people feel that they are welcome [and that] this is their museum," Humphrey said. caught flack since renderings were released last month. I called the proposed building "<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/09/21/griffin-museum-science-industry-design-ramsa-drawing-board" target="_blank" >a big old wide-brimmed hat blocking the screen at the movie theater</a>."</p><p>Others have criticized the building too, including noted Chicago author and historian Tim Samuelson. </p><p>In a Sun-Times <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/09/23/griffin-museum-of-science-and-industry-cta-artificial-intelligence-ai" target="_blank" >letter to the editor</a>, Samuelson said the hall and the museum's new South Portico renovation "display gross disrespect for a masterpiece ... nearly perfect in composition, proportions and detail."</p><p>I've got no beef with the South Portico project. Sure, it's a secondary entrance, but it shows restraint and a sense of proportion that the Welcome Hall lacks.</p><p>Ramsey said the hall "creates this sense of welcome for people who are not necessarily architecture buffs, who don't necessarily have the same appreciation for very strict, and some would say, forbidding, classical architecture."</p><p>The seven previously considered Welcome Hall images I saw were not as elaborately rendered as the approved design, so its hard to say which of them might have been a better alternative.</p><p>But the renderings do show the Griffin MSI and RAMSA at least considered more purely glass designs. Some that — to my eye at least — resembled the transparency of the <a class="Link" href="https://inhabitat.com/glassy-renovation-brings-natural-light-into-canadian-museum-of-nature/" target="_blank" >2010 addition</a> atop Ottawa's century-old Canadian Museum of Nature, or the Portland Art Museum's 22,000-square-foot Mark Rothko <a class="Link" href="https://portlandartmuseum.org/campus-transformation/" target="_blank" >entrance pavilion.</a></p><p>"There was no stone unturned, in terms of different architectural ideas," Getman
